newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH ELECTION VIEW UPDATE - MARKET COMMENT.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH ELECTION VIEW UPDATE - MARKET COMMENT.

text.p: The following is an update of comments from analysts in financial markets after a runoff vote in France's parliamentary election pointing to a victory for the left.
ERIC MULLER, ECONOMIST, UBS, PARIS

There is a demand for a change in policies on the economy and on Europe. There is also budgetary uncertainty. More and more this campaign has shown on consensus on the desire to look at (Maastricht treaty) criteria in terms of trend. The share market has priced in the risk to the euro more than the bond market.
PAUL HORNE, ECONOMIST, SMITH BARNEY, PARIS

The odds are that (Socialist party leader Lionel) Jospin will want to make the euro more and more of a marshmalllow. The Socialists want a weak euro...with less budgetary discipline, wider and less credible membership in EMU. That is precisely what German citizens are most worried about.
JEAN-FRANCOIS MERCIER, ECONOMIST, SALOMON BROTHERS, LONDON

I would expect the Socialists to definitely govern with an eye on financial markets. They have made statements in the past week trying to reassure the markets about their commitment to fiscal discipline.
ERIC CHANEY, ECONOMIST, MORGAN STANLEY, PARIS

The main reaction will be that all this is bad for core European assets and we are going to see higher long bond yields for everybody. I don't know if the (10-year bond yield) spread between France and Germany will move. If the market goes down French investors will buy. I expect the currency to be under pressure and of course the short end of the market.
I think markets will react by implicitly raising the possibility of an EMU delay on the back of the ambiguities about what has been said tonight.
SONJA GIBBS, BOND ANALYST, NOMURA, LONDON
The initial reaction may be to dump Europe all together - then in a few weeks if EMU is still in jeopardy, if the German government continues to tear itself apart, I would buy the mark.
MARK GEDDES, TREASURY ECONOMIST ABN-AMRO, LONDON

French markets are likely to come under some pressure early on this week. On mark/Paris, over last few weeks we have had some pretty aggressive Bank of France action to try to limit the downside, and I'll expect that to be intensified.

Looking further ahead, the implications of a Socialist victory with respect to...EMU going ahead on time are potentially more profound and will have a bigger impact on French markets. If Jospin were to push Germany too far on issues like renegotiating the stability pact or Italian membership then that raises the whole prospect of a delay.

What you'll probably find in the short-term is a damage limitation exercise from the politicians to try and keep alive the idea EMU is going ahead on time. The political will for EMU to survive is still very strong.
DARREN WILLIAMS, INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIST, UBS, LONDON:
I'm not sure on European monetary union whether the Socialists are any worse than (Philippe) Seguin (seen as a could-be centre-right prime minister if the right had won).
There's a terrific amount of uncertainty on how the cohabitation (between left government and conservative President Jacques Chirac) is going to pan out.
France has been buffetted for some time now by fiscal and EMU questions. They're in for it again just when they didn't need it.
ELISABETTA CASTELLI, HEAD INT'L EQUITIES, CDC BOURSE, PARIS:
Although the uncertainty has been taken away on the election result, we really do not know what the programme is.

What we've heard is of concern to the financial markets. We don't know whether France Telecom and Thomson-CSF will be privatised. How are they going to get the budget deficit down? Will they delay entry into the euro?
There will be considerable volatility as announcements come through on policy decisions.
THOMAS MAYER, ECONOMIST, GOLDMAN SACHS.

In both countries, Germany and France, fiscal consolidation and austerity is going to be very difficult. In Germany we have the gold row and right now there is an emergency meeting about the 1998 budget.
The message out of France is that the French electorate is also resisting stronger fiscal austerity. But there is also some relief that the pro-EMU faction won.

We probably cannot count on as much fiscal consolidation and tightening as just a few months ago and this is not very good news for European bond markets which were counting on significant consolidation.
The risks for EMU have increased somewhat but I still don't believe that the EMU process is going to be derailed. Remember it was the Socialists who negotiated the Maastricht treaty.
ECKHARD SCHULTE, ECONOMIST, IBJ
It's looking as if the conservative era is coming to an end.
I think many people in Germany will now discuss the euro much more intensively than they have done so far.
The most important question from the German point of view is, is France still a partner to execute monetary union?

We have to wait and see what programme the Socialists come up with. I do not doubt the Socialists will go into the euro but probably not with (a budget deficit of) 3.0 percent (of gross domestic product) and probably not with a core euro (narrow membership). That is the decisive question. I think they still will follow EMU, but they would like to fudge the criteria.
The majority of voters decided to elect a party which favours a fudge and a broad EMU. It's now fudge or delay. The ball is in the German camp.
-- Paris Newsroom +33 1 42 21 53 81
